newsitem.title: FRANCE: French TV stocks said reflecting ownership fears.
newsitem.headline: French TV stocks said reflecting ownership fears.

text.p: Worries over possible changes to laws governing ownership of French media companies are already reflected in the companies' share price, dealers said on Tuesday.
Shares in companies with communications interests dipped, but were mostly off less than the overall market in late morning trade.

Generale des Eaux, cable TV operator and the main shareholder of Havas, slipped 18 francs to 710, Bouygues, which holds 39 percent of TF1, lost three to 518, while Lyonnaise des Eaux, parent of Lyonnaise Cable, also shed three to 536 at 1043 GMT.

Havas, which holds 34.4 percent of pay TV company Canal Plus, was 5.20 francs lower at 400.80, while Canal Plus lost 14 to 1,005. TF1 was just one franc off at 537. The CAC-40 index was 0.62 percent lower at 2,669.42.

The market had expected TV stocks to be hit after comments on Sunday by Catherine Trautmann, France's new Communication and Culture Minister, that France did not have sufficiently strong anti-trust laws to prevent concentration of ownership.
"The most important point is limiting concentration. In all European countries there are anti-trust laws which are more or less efficient," Trautmann told a weekly debate on RTL television and radio.

Trautmann said the new government wants to bring back a previous 25 percent limit on ownership by a single shareholder of media companies. The previous centre-right government had increased this limit to 49 percent.

"For the moment we do not have a sufficiently clear and efficient system in France, notably in relation to investment by companies which win public contracts, and which can today intervene in a quasi-majority way. We want to bring back the 25 percent limit," she said.

She also said she wanted to review an accord under which public television channels France 2 and France 3 are broadcast exclusively on digital satellite service Television par Satellite (TPS), operated by TF1.
If such an exclusive deal were to be outlawed, France 2 and France 3 would also be broadcast on rival satellite service Canalsatellite, owned by Canal Plus.
